Replication of Karlan and List (2007)

Social Information and Charitable Giving

Author

Wanxing Dai

Published

April 22, 2026

Introduction

Karlan and List (2007) study whether social and behavioral factors can influence charitable giving. The authors conduct a large-scale field experiment in which potential donors receive different types of solicitation letters. The goal is to understand how the treatment affects both the likelihood of donating and the amount donated.

Because individuals are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups, the experiment allows the authors to estimate causal effects. If the treatment and control groups look similar at baseline, then later differences in giving behavior can be interpreted as the effect of the treatment itself.

Main Analysis

I begin by checking whether treatment and control groups are balanced on observable baseline characteristics. This reproduces the logic of Table 1 in the paper.

aggregate(
  cbind(years, female, couple, redcty, bluecty, dormant, ltmedMRA) ~ treatment,
  data = data,
  FUN = mean
)

The means are very similar across the two groups, which suggests that the randomization was successful and that there is no obvious evidence of selection bias.

Next, I replicate the main treatment effect results from Table 2A by estimating how the treatment affects the probability of giving and the amount donated.

summary(lm(gave ~ treatment, data = data))

The treatment has a positive and statistically significant effect on the probability of making a donation. The estimated coefficient on treatment is about 0.0042, with a p-value below 0.01. This implies that treated individuals were more likely to donate than individuals in the control group.

For donation amount, the estimated treatment effect is also positive, around 0.154, but it is only marginally statistically significant. This suggests that treatment may increase average donation size, but the evidence is weaker than for the extensive-margin effect on whether a person donates at all.

Something Additional

As an additional analysis, I present a graphical comparison of donation amounts in the treatment and control groups.

boxplot(
  amount ~ treatment,
  data = data,
  main = "Donation Amount by Treatment Status",
  xlab = "Treatment Group",
  ylab = "Donation Amount"
)

The figure shows that donation amounts are somewhat higher in the treatment group, which is broadly consistent with the regression results. While the difference is not dramatic, the graph helps visualize the direction of the treatment effect.

Overall, this replication confirms the main idea of the paper. Random assignment creates comparable groups, and the treatment increases the likelihood of giving. This is what allows the authors to make a causal claim about the effect of the solicitation treatment.
